image.alt: A Philodendron Pink Princess in a white pot, its dark leaves marked with bright pink on deep red stems

light.label: Bright indirect light
light.note: Tolerates medium light, but the pink fades and new leaves come back plain green

landscape_use.note: Frost-free zones, never in direct sun

snap: A climbing Philodendron with deep green, almost black leaves splashed in bright pink, carried on dark red stems. Every leaf is marked differently. It needs bright, filtered light to keep the pink, and is toxic to cats and dogs if chewed.

deep_dive.title: Origin & Habit
deep_dive.body: A cultivated form of Philodendron erubescens, a climbing aroid from the rainforests of South America. It climbs as it matures and does its best work up a moss pole, where the leaves grow larger with each new one.

deep_dive.title: Key Care Rule
deep_dive.body: Water when the top inch of the mix has dried, in a loose, chunky aroid mix — these roots rot fast in heavy soil. Bright filtered light is what keeps the pink coming; in a dim corner the new leaves revert to plain green, and direct sun scorches the pink parts first.

deep_dive.title: Special Feature
deep_dive.body: The pink is unstable, so no two leaves match and the plant needs steering: a stem throwing only green leaves is cut back to a pink node, and an all-pink leaf has no green left to feed itself and will eventually fail. Not to be confused with Pink Congo, whose pink is chemically induced and turns green for good after a few months.

deep_dive.title: Pet Safety
deep_dive.body: Toxic to cats and dogs if chewed or swallowed; like all philodendrons it carries calcium oxalate crystals that irritate the mouth and stomach. Keep it up on a shelf if pets chew at leaves.
